Date: 2026-10-21
Time: 15:05 - 16:02 UTC
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Leah Chen (Redwood SE), Jordan Ortiz (Redwood solutions), Elena Ruiz (Morningstar Head of ML), Marc D'Souza (Platform), Priya Kapoor (CTO), Tomas Berg (SRE)
summary: Initial discovery focused on how Morningstar's constrained budget and variable burst traffic would map to Redwood's hosted vs dedicated vs private options. Key themes: per-token unit economics, batching and KV cache levers, fallback policies, and network/VPC constraints for a regulated client. Customer is curious about predictable monthly spend and whether a hybrid hosting mix (hosted baseline + dedicated for peak) makes sense.
topics: current stack & telemetry (how many tokens per request, sequences)
batching and cold-start KV cache behavior
hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs and price predictability
transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick round of intros?
[00:08] Elena: Hi, Elena Ruiz, head of ML at Morningstar.
[00:12] Marc: Marc D'Souza, platform engineering, I own infra.
[00:15] Priya: Priya Kapoor, CTO.
[00:18] Tomas: Tomas, SRE.
[00:21] Samir: Great, Samir Patel here, AE at Redwood, and Leah Chen is our SE who will dig into perf details.
[00:28] Leah: Hi all. Quick agenda — understand load shape and cost constraints, then we can talk levers: batching, kv cache, quantization, and hosting mix.
[00:38] Elena: Sounds good. To set context, we have an internal product with a hard monthly budget cap, like real hard. We need sub-100ms median latency for a small % of calls, but most are batch-ish around 700-1200 tokens. Our spikes from analytics can double throughput for 10-15 minutes.
[00:56] Samir: OK so bursty with a few low-latency critical paths. Are those critical calls long or short?
[01:03] Elena: Short — 60 to 120 tokens. The rest are longer, 500-1,200 tokens for summarization.
[01:10] Marc: Our infra team wants predictable spend; if a spike happens we can't blow the monthly cap. We asked vendors how they handle throttles and fallbacks.
[01:18] Samir: Makes sense. Two quick things: per-token pricing is one lever, but so are batching (more throughput for same token price) and KV cache to reduce repeated context costs. Also routing to cheaper model variants during spikes is an option.
[01:30] Priya: Can you explain how KV cache reduces costs? We saw a doc that mentioned prefix caching but the terms were fuzzy.
[01:36] Leah: Sure. Basically when you're streaming a long session, the KV cache stores past key/value states so later tokens don't re-compute the full prefix attention. For many of your long summarization calls, if you can split prompts into reusable prefixes we can cache those and the per-inference work drops substantially. In practice you'll see big drop in per-token compute for repeated prefixes.
[01:56] Elena: Right but our prompts are quite dynamic — not lots of exact repeats. How tolerant is the cache?
[02:02] Leah: Good question. Cache wins when there's repeated substrings or predictable system prompt. If it's fully bespoke each time, KV cache helps less. But there are middle grounds — we can cache common instruction blocks and system messages. Also our prefix-KV can sometimes be used across sessions for templated flows.
[02:18] Marc: And batching — how much does it affect latency vs cost? We run synchronous APIs, so we care about tail latency.
[02:25] Leah: Batching increases throughput by packing tokens across concurrent requests. If your traffic is bursty, batching during bursts is efficient. But batching does add queuing latency — typical trade: with dynamic batching you can target a tail SLO. For sub-100ms calls we recommend carving those to dedicated low-latency pool, and let the hosted pool batch the rest.
[02:43] Samir: Another angle is hybrid routing: tagged low-latency calls go to dedicated/gold pool (higher unit cost but lower latency), and background summarizations go to hosted with batching and higher quantization for cost savings.
[02:54] Priya: What's the rough delta in per-token cost between hosted and dedicated? We need numbers to present to finance.
[03:01] Samir: I'll share exact worksheet, but ballpark: hosted baseline with our open model variants is lowest list price, but dedicated committed capacity reduces per-token at scale — however committed is OPEX/CapEx trade. For many customers, a hosted+dedicated burst mix is best — hosted handles baseline, dedicated covers predictable steady throughput or guaranteed SLOs.
[03:20] Elena: Can you give a concrete example: say 200k tokens/day, 90% long summarizations, 10% low-latency. How would cost shape?
[03:29] Leah: Off top of my head, if you had 180k tokens/day long calls and used batching + KV cache on say 40% of those, effective tokens billed drop and compute per token drops — maybe a 30-50% perf/cost win depending on cache hit rate. The 20k low-latency tokens going to dedicated might cost 1.5–2x per token but keep tail latency low. We'll do a sim with your real hist.
[03:50] Marc: We need predictable monthly spend. Do you offer hard caps or throttles? What happens when tokens exceed quota?
[03:58] Samir: We have quota controls and rate limiting. You can set soft limits with alerts and hard cutoffs. We also have fallbacks configured to return a lighter model or queued response. Customers often set a policy: degrade to a distilled model first, then to cached response, then fail open if necessary.
[04:18] Tomas: Network constraints — we may need VPC peering and egress blacklists. Does Redwood hosted allow peered VPC or do we need Private?
[04:26] Samir: Hosted API does not live in your VPC. For VPC peering and strict egress controls, Redwood Private (or Dedicated in your VPC via dedicated private connectors) is recommended. There's also a gateway option for hybrid setups.
[04:38] Priya: Security posture — KMS integration, audit logs?
[04:41] Leah: We support customer-managed keys (KMS) for Private, and audit logs and token-level tracing in the Console. Hosted offers encrypted-at-rest, SOC2, but customer KMS is off by default unless on Private.
[04:55] Elena: For early pilot we prefer hosted but need assurances around data retention and export controls.
[04:59] Samir: We can provide our security pack and a data retention SLA. I'll attach both.
[05:05] [05:05] Elena: Quick Q: how does quantization effect model quality for summarization?
[05:10] Leah: Our quantization stack is tuned per-model. For many summarization tasks, 4-bit quant gives negligible quality loss if you tune prompts. But if you are hitting factuality-sensitive outputs you may want higher-precision for those routes. We can profile.
[05:23] Marc: About benching — can you run with our sample payload? We'll share 5k requests with real token distributions.
[05:30] Leah: Absolutely. If you drop the histogram and a few prompt templates we can run a 48-hour throughput sim and return latency, batch sizes, and effective token burn.
[05:40] Elena: We'll do that. Also curious about billing — do you bill for tokens before cache subtraction or net tokens after caching/batching?
[05:48] Samir: Good nuance. Billing is on net-served tokens; if KV cache removes work for repeated ranges we may only bill for incremental tokens. Batching itself doesn't change token count billed but reduces compute cost, which is reflected in pricing tiers or dedicated capacity math.
[06:03] Tomas: I've heard transcripts mis-report KV as K V cash — we need you to include clear diagrams because some of our execs are not deep in ML.
[06:10] Samir: We'll include a short diagram and a one-pager on KV cache semantics.
[06:14] Priya: Competitors — we've looked at Anthropic and a few self-host routes. Any notable differences we should highlight?
[06:20] Samir: The big difference is our runtime: we eke out cost with continuous batching, cache-aware scheduling, and model-variant routing. Anthropic and others have different SLA/cost tradeoffs; self-host gives control but big ops. We'll include a short comparison table.
[06:32] Elena: About fallback policies — if we route to a distilled model for budget, how do we measure quality regression? We need an eval hook.
[06:39] Leah: Redwood Optimize ties eval sets to rollouts — you can define prompt sets and quality thresholds. If performance drops we can auto-failover. We'll show you the UI in the pilot.
[06:50] Marc: Pilot terms — what does a pilot look like? Committed tokens for 30 days? Free credits?
[06:56] Samir: We typically do a 30–60 day pilot: free credits for initial testing and a small reserved capacity if you want baseline SLOs. If you need dedicated reserved capacity for latency we can discuss a short-term contract. We'll include options in the worksheet.
[07:10] Elena: One last perf Q — cold KV cache: how long does it warm? If we have a 10-minute burst, will cache warm in time to help?
[07:18] Leah: If your usage is many unique sessions, warming might be limited. But if you have templated prompts or repeated components, warm-up can be quick. Also we can pre-populate cache for planned events by seeding common prefixes.
[07:31] [07:31] Samir: OK, recap: Redwood to send pricing worksheet + security pack + KV cache one-pager. SE will run throughput sim after Morningstar sends sample prompts and hist. Customer to decide pilot scope. Anything else?
[07:45] Priya: Please call out explicit hard-cap behavior and the sequence of fallback policies in writing.
[07:51] Samir: Will do.
[07:54] Elena: Thanks, that's helpful. Looking forward to the worksheet.
[07:58] Samir: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the doc bundle and a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff.
[08:05] [end — notes: periods in transcript denote approximate times; some timestamps skipped for brevity]
